title: Seeing the Wood for the Trees
author: Haili Hughes
summary: Hughes examines why school leaders lose sight of the whole, and names the cognitive biases that make it predictable: optimism bias inflating how well things are going, the bias blind spot letting leaders see flaws in others but not themselves, and illusory superiority producing both overrating of one's own school and the belief that a context is too unique to learn from anyone. She supplies her own failure as evidence, refusing advice to update an English curriculum she had poured herself into while outcomes stayed poor and the department went into special measures. The forest metaphor carries the argument: the trees are staff absence, parent complaints, safeguarding alerts, each legitimately urgent, while the wood is the school's overall health and direction, and a school can manage the first superbly while stagnating in teaching, curriculum or culture. Her hardest point is about persistence, which she argues slips into stubbornness when leaders double down on a marking policy that consumes evenings without shifting learning. The remedies are external eyes that disrupt complacency, a culture where staff can raise concerns without fear, and metacognitive questions that interrogate one's own reasoning.
points: The biases are named specifically rather than gestured at: optimism bias, the bias blind spot, and illusory superiority, each with a distinct effect on how leaders read their own schools.
The self-evaluation evidence is the concrete hook, with leaders reliably rating their schools more highly than external inspectors do.
The forest metaphor separates two legitimate jobs, handling urgent daily concerns and holding the school's direction, and shows a school can do the first well while stagnating.
The persistence point is the uncomfortable one: staying the course is celebrated as a virtue and becomes stubbornness once evidence of failure is available and refused.
The three metacognitive questions are directly usable, particularly whether an approach is being retained because it works or because it is familiar.
quotes: A common problem in leadership is that we are often so absorbed in the day-to-day detail that it becomes difficult to step back, reflect and identify the bigger picture.
The optimism bias for example, leads us to believe things are going better than they are (Sharot, 2011).
When conducting self-evaluations, for instance, leaders often rate their schools more highly than external inspectors do (Chapman, 2000).
But when leaders focus exclusively on the trees, they risk losing sight of the wood: the overall health and direction of the school.
But persistence can slip into stubbornness if leaders are unwilling to acknowledge failure.
But sometimes, the courageous move is not to push harder, but to do things differently.
True leadership lies not in defending the status quo at all costs but in having the humility to adapt.
